description: English translations of the passages in Latin, Greek and other languages than French. at: the passage in the unit (part, start, end); lang: ISO 639 code; text: the passage; translation: English; source: the author and work quoted, where the edition names them; note: a misprint or a doubtful reading. Candidates found by a character-trigram model (Latin, French, English) and Greek letters; passages fixed and translated by Claude Opus; not checked by hand.

items.text: Jus à jubendo : Jura enim veteres jusa vel jussa vocabant. Festus : Jussæ Jura.
items.translation: Jus [right, law] comes from jubere [to command]: for the ancients called jura [laws] 'jusa' or 'jussa' [things commanded]. Festus: 'jussae', laws.
items.note: The Latin is an etymology linking jus/jura with jubere, jussum (to command, a command), so the Latin forms are kept in the translation.

items.text: Huic respondebimus, nunquam expectare nos certissimam rerum compre- »hensionem : quoniam in arduo est veri exploratio : sed eâ ire, quâ ducit veri si- »militudo. OMNE HAC VIA PROCEDIT OFFICIUM. Sic serimus, sic navigamus, sic »militamus, sic uxores ducimus, sic liberos tollimus ; quam omnium horum incertus »sit eventus. Ad ea accedimus, de quibus bené sperandum esse credimus. Quis »enim polliceatur serenti proventum, naviganti portum, militanti victoriam, mari- »to pudicam uxorem, patri pios liberos ? Sequimur qua RATIO, non qua veri- »tas trahit. EXSPECTA, UT NISI BENE CESSURA NON FACIAS, ET »NISI COMPERTA VERITATE NIHIL MOVERIS : RELICTO OMNI »ACTU VITA CONSISTIT. Dum verisimilia me in hoc aut illud impellant, »non verebor beneficium dare ei quem verisimile erit gratum esse.
items.translation: To him we shall answer that we never wait for a perfectly certain grasp of things, since the search for truth is arduous, but go the way that probability leads. Every duty proceeds by this path. So we sow, so we sail, so we go to war, so we take wives, so we raise children, though the outcome of all these things is uncertain. We undertake those things for which we believe there is good ground for hope. For who would guarantee the sower a harvest, the sailor a harbour, the soldier victory, the husband a chaste wife, the father dutiful children? We follow where reason, not where truth, draws us. Wait until you do nothing that will not turn out well, and make no move until the truth is established: then all action is abandoned and life stands still. So long as probabilities urge me this way or that, I shall not be afraid to give a benefit to one who will probably be grateful.
items.note: 'quam omnium horum incertus sit eventus' appears to be a misprint for 'cum' (as in Seneca's text), here translated 'though'.

items.text: Obligatio à ligando.
items.translation: Obligatio [obligation] from ligare [to bind].
items.note: An etymology: the Latin words are kept in the translation.

items.text: Qui in utero est, perinde ac si in rebus humanis esset, custoditur, quotiens de commodo ipsius partus, quæritur.
items.translation: One who is in the womb is protected just as if he were among the living, whenever the advantage of the unborn child itself is in question.
items.note: The edition's reference 'Tit. 3' is an error for title 5 of Book I of the Digest.

items.text: Itaque pati quis injuriam, etiam si non sentiat, potest : facere nemo, nisi qui scit se injuriam facere, etiamsi nesciat cui faciat.
items.translation: Thus a person can suffer a wrong even if he does not perceive it; but no one can commit one unless he knows that he is committing a wrong, even if he does not know against whom he commits it.
items.note: 'Injuria' is the Roman delict of outrage or insult, rendered here as 'wrong'.

items.text: Regula est, Juris quidem ignorantiam cuique nocere.
items.translation: The rule is that ignorance of the law is prejudicial to everyone.
items.source: Digest XXII.6.9 pr. (De juris et facti ignorantia)

items.text: Ex quo etiam intelligitur omni Legi civili annexam esse pœnam, vel ex- »plicitè, vel implicitè ; Nam ubi pœna neque scripto, neque exemplo alicujus »qui pœnas Legis jam transgressæ dedit, definitur ; ibi subintelligitur pœnam arbitrarium esse, nimirum ex arbitrio pendere Legislatoris.
items.translation: From this it is also understood that a penalty is attached to every civil law, either explicitly or implicitly; for where the penalty is fixed neither in writing nor by the example of someone who has already paid the penalty for breaking the law, there it is understood that the penalty is arbitrary, that is, depends on the discretion of the legislator.
items.note: 'arbitrarium' is a misprint for 'arbitrariam', agreeing with 'pœnam'.

items.text: Nam quæ facta lædunt pietatem, existimationem, verecundiam nostram, & (ut generaliter dixerim) contra bonos mores fiunt, nec facere nos posse credendum est.
items.translation: For acts which offend our dutiful affection, our reputation, our sense of shame, and (to speak generally) which are done against good morals, must be held to be things we cannot do.

items.text: Jus rectorium & æquatorium
items.translation: Rectorial and equatorial right (the right of a superior over inferiors, and the right that holds between equals).
items.source: Grotius, De jure belli ac pacis I.1.3

items.text: Agnitio verò unici, æterni, infiniti, omnipotentis Dei, ab investiga- «tione Causarum, virtutum operationumque Corporum naturalium, quàm à cura «futuri temporis, faciliùs derivari potuit. Nam qui ab effectu quocunque, quem «viderit, ad Causam ejus proximam ratiocinaretur, & inde ad illius Causæ Cau- «sam proximam procederet, & in Causarum deinceps ordinem profundè se im- «mergeret, inveniret tandem (cum veterum Philosophorum sanioribus) unicum «esse Primum Motorem, id est, unicam & æternam rerum omnium Causam, «quam appellant omnes DEUM.
items.translation: But the knowledge of one, eternal, infinite, omnipotent God could more easily be derived from investigating the causes, powers and operations of natural bodies than from anxiety about the future. For whoever reasoned from any effect he had seen to its nearest cause, and from there went on to the nearest cause of that cause, and plunged deep into the succession of causes, would at last find (with the sounder of the ancient philosophers) that there is one First Mover, that is, one eternal cause of all things, which all men call God.

items.text: Hæc (Philosophia) nos primùm ad illorum (Deorum) cultum, deinde ad jus hominum, quod situm est in Generis humani Societate, tum ad modestiam magnitudinemque animi erudivit.
items.translation: She (Philosophy) has taught us first the worship of them (the gods), then the right of men, which rests on the society of the human race, and then moderation and greatness of mind.

items.text: Quo alio tuti sumus quàm quòd mutuis juvamur officiis ? Hoc uno instruc- »tior vita, contràque incursiones subitas, munitior est, beneficiorum commercio. Fac »nos singulos, quid sumus ? præda animalium & victimæ, ac bellissimus & facilli- »mus sanguis. Quoniam cæteris animalibus in tutelam sui satis virium est : quæ- »cunque vaga nascuntur, & actura vitam segregem, armata sunt. Hominem im- »becillitas cingit ; non unguium vis, non dentium, terribilem cæteris fecit. Nu- »dum & infirmum societas munit. Duas res dedit quæ illum, obnoxium cæteris, »validissimum facerent, rationem & societatem. Itaque, qui par esse nulli posset »si seduceretur, rerum potitur. Societas illi dominium omnium animalium dedit. »Societas terris genitum, in alienæ naturæ, transmisit imperium, & dominari etiam »in mari jussit. Hæc morborum impetus arcuit, senectuti adminicula prospexit, »solatia contrà dolores dedit. Hæc fortes nos facit, quod licet contrà fortunam »advocare. Hanc societatem tolle, & unitatem generis humani, quâ vita susti- »netur, scindes.
items.translation: By what else are we safe than by helping one another with mutual services? By this one thing, the exchange of benefits, life is better equipped and better fortified against sudden attacks. Take us one by one: what are we? The prey and the victims of animals, and blood most choice and most easily shed. For the other animals have strength enough to protect themselves: all that are born to roam and to lead a solitary life are armed. Man is surrounded by weakness; no strength of claws or of teeth has made him fearsome to others. Naked and weak as he is, society fortifies him. [Nature] gave him two things which made him, otherwise at the mercy of the rest, the strongest of all: reason and society. So he who could be a match for no one, if he were left apart, becomes master of the world. Society has given him dominion over all animals; society has carried him, born on land, into the dominion of an alien element and bidden him rule even over the sea. It has checked the onslaught of diseases, provided supports for old age, and given comfort against sorrows. It makes us brave, because we may call on it against fortune. Take away this society, and you will tear apart the unity of the human race, by which life is sustained.

items.text: Homo sum ; humani nihil à me alienum puto.
items.translation: I am a man; I consider nothing human foreign to me.

items.text: Ut ridentibus adrident, ita flentibus adsunt Humani vultus.
items.translation: As human faces smile on those who smile, so they attend on those who weep.
items.note: Most editions of Horace read 'adflent' (weep with) where this text has 'adsunt'.

items.text: Sed quoniam, (ut præclare scriptum est à Platone,) Non nobis solùm »nati sumus, ortûsque nostri partem patria vindicat, partem amici : atque, (ut »placet Stoïcis ) quæ in terris gignuntur, ad usum hominum omnia creari, homi- »nes autem hominum causa esse generatos, ut ipsi inter se aliis alii prodesse pos- »sent : in hoc Naturam debemus ducem sequi, & communes utilitates in medium »afferre, mutatione officiorum, dando, accipiendo : tum artibus, tum operâ, tum »facultatibus devincire hominum inter homines societatem.
items.translation: But since (as Plato has admirably written) we are not born for ourselves alone, but our country claims a share of our existence and our friends a share; and since (as the Stoics hold) all that the earth produces is created for the use of men, while men are born for the sake of men, so that they may be able to help one another: in this we ought to follow Nature as our guide, contribute to the common stock what serves the common good by an exchange of services, by giving and receiving, and by our skills, our labour and our means bind fast the society of men with one another.

items.text: Est quidem vera Lex, recta Ratio, naturæ congruens, d'ffusa in omnes, »constans, sempiterna, quæ vocet ad officium jubendo, vetando à fraude deter- »reat : quæ tamen neque probos frustra jubet, aut vetat ; nec improbos jubendo »aut vetando movet. Huic Legi nec obrogari fas est, neque derogari ex hac ali- »quid licet ; neque tota abrogari potest. Nec verò aut per Senatum , aut per »Populum solvi hac Lege possumus : neque est quærendus explanator, aut inter- »pres ejus alius. Nec erit alia Lex Romæ, alia Athenis, alia nunc, alia posthac ; sed »omnes Gentes, & omni tempore, una Lex , & sempiterna & inmutabilis conti- »nebit ; unusque erit communis quasi Magister & Imperator omnium DEUS. »Ille Legis hujus inventor, disceptator, lator : cui qui non parebit, ipse se fugiet, »ac naturam hominis aspernabitur ; atque hoc ipso luet maximas pœnas , etiamsi »cætera supplicia , quæ putantur, effugerit.
items.translation: There is indeed a true law, right reason, in agreement with nature, spread among all men, constant, everlasting, which summons to duty by its commands and deters from wrongdoing by its prohibitions; and which yet neither commands nor forbids good men in vain, nor moves the wicked by commanding or forbidding. It is not lawful to pass laws against this law, nor is it permitted to take away any part of it, nor can it be repealed as a whole. Nor can we be released from this law by the Senate or by the People, nor need any other expounder or interpreter of it be sought. There will not be one law at Rome and another at Athens, one now and another hereafter, but one law, everlasting and unchangeable, will bind all nations and at all times; and there will be one common master, as it were, and ruler of all, God. He is the author of this law, its judge, and its proposer: whoever will not obey it will flee from himself and spurn the nature of man, and by this very fact will pay the heaviest penalties, even if he escapes the other things that are counted punishments.
items.source: Cicero, De re publica III, quoted by Lactantius, Divinae institutiones VI.8

items.text: Ne- »que verò hoc solum Naturâ, id est, Jure Gentium ..... constitutum est, ut non »liceat sui commodi causâ, alteri nocere.
items.translation: Nor indeed is it established by nature alone, that is, by the law of nations ..... that it is not permitted to harm another for the sake of one's own advantage.
items.note: The ellipsis replaces Cicero's words "but also by the laws of peoples" (sed etiam legibus populorum), left out by Burlamaqui.

items.text: Nemo sibi debet
items.translation: No one is in debt to himself.

items.text: hoc verbum »debere non habet nisi inter duos locum.
items.translation: This word "to owe" has no place except between two [persons].

items.text: In quo lapsa consuetudo deflexit de via, sensimque eò deducta est, ut »honestatem ab utilitate secernens, & constituerit honestum esse aliquod quod »utile non esset & utile, quod non honestum : quâ nulla pernicies major homi- »num vitæ potuit adferri.
items.translation: On this point custom slipped and strayed from the path, and was gradually brought to the point where, separating the honourable from the useful, it laid down that something could be honourable that was not useful, and useful that was not honourable: no greater plague than this could have been brought upon human life.
items.note: The printed "& constituerit" stands for Cicero's "constitueret"; the sense is unaffected.

items.text: Itaque accepimus, SOCRA- »TEM exsecrari solitum eos, qui primum hæc naturâ cohærentia opinione distra- »xissent.
items.translation: And so we are told that Socrates used to curse those who first pulled apart in opinion these things that are joined together by nature.

items.text: Exemplo quodcunque malo committitur, ipsi »Displicet auctori : Prima hæc est ultio, quod, se »Judice, nemo nocens absolvitur, improba quamvis »Gratia fallaci Prætoris vicerit Urnâ.
items.translation: Whatever is done that sets a bad example displeases its very author: this is the first vengeance, that with himself as judge no guilty man is acquitted, even though the wicked favour of the praetor has won the day through the deceitful urn.
items.note: The urn is the voting urn of the praetor's court, rigged by favour.

items.text: Ambiguæ si quando citabere testis Incertæque rei : Phalaris licet imperet, ut fis Falsus, & admoto dictet perjuria tauro, Summum crede nefas animam præferre pudori, Et propter vitam vivendi perdere causas.
items.translation: If ever you are summoned as witness in a doubtful and uncertain matter, though Phalaris should command you to be false and, bringing up his bull, dictate perjuries to you, believe it the greatest wickedness to prefer life to honour, and for the sake of life to lose the reasons for living.

items.text: Quemadmodum Attalus noster dicere solebat, Malitia »ipsa maximam partem veneni sui bibit.
items.translation: As our Attalus used to say, malice itself drinks the greater part of its own poison.
items.source: Seneca, Letters to Lucilius (cited as Ep. 82)
items.note: In modern editions the passage is in Letter 81 (§22).

items.text: Animorum nulla in terris origo inveniri potest: nihil enim est in ani- «mis mixtum atque concretum, aut quod ex terrâ natum atque fictum esse vi- «deatur ; nihil ne aut humidum quidem aut flabile aut igneum. His enim in «naturis nihil inest, quod vim memoriæ, mentis, cogitationis habeat ; quod & «præterita teneat & futura provideat & complecti possit præsentia : quæ sola di- «vina sunt ; nec invenietur unquam, unde ad hominem venire possint, nisi à «DEO. Singularis est igitur quædam natura atque vis animi, sejuncta ab his «usitatis notisque naturis. Ita quicquid est illud, quod sentit, quod sapit, quod «vivit, quod viget, cœleste & divinum, ob eamque rem æternum sit necesse est.
items.translation: No origin of souls can be found on earth: for there is nothing in souls mixed or compounded, or that seems to have been born or formed out of earth; nothing even moist, or airy, or fiery. For in these natures there is nothing that has the power of memory, of mind, of thought; that holds the past, foresees the future and can take in the present: which things alone are divine; nor will it ever be found whence they could come to man, except from God. There is therefore a singular nature and power of the soul, separate from these common and known natures. Thus whatever it is that feels, that knows, that lives, that is active, must be heavenly and divine, and for that reason eternal.

items.text: Quid multa ? Sic mihi persuasi, sic sentio, cùm tanta celeritas animo- «rum sit, tanta memoria præteritorum, futurorumque prudentia, tot artes, tantæ «scientiæ, tot inventa, non posse eam naturam, quæ res eas contineat, esse «mortalem.
items.translation: In short, this is my conviction, this is what I feel: since the swiftness of souls is so great, the memory of things past and the foresight of things to come so great, so many arts, so many sciences, so many discoveries, the nature that contains these things cannot be mortal.

items.text: Nemo unquam sine magna spe immortalitatis se pro Patria offerret ad mortem. Licuit esse otioso Themistocli ; licuit Epaminondæ ; licuit , ne & vetera & externa quæram, mihi : sed nescio quo modo inhæret in mentibus quasi sæculorum quoddam augurium futurorum ; idque in maximis ingeniis altissimisque animis existit maximè, & apparet facillimè. Quo quidem dempto, quis tam esset amens, qui semper in laboribus & periculis viveret ?
items.translation: No one would ever offer himself to death for his country without a great hope of immortality. Themistocles could have lived at ease; so could Epaminondas; so could I, not to look for ancient and foreign examples: but somehow there clings in men's minds a kind of presentiment of ages to come; and this is strongest and shows itself most readily in the greatest minds and loftiest souls. Take it away, and who would be so mad as to live always amid toils and dangers?
